entity.name: Li Bai
entity.description: The drunken sword-fighting poet China calls the Immortal of Poetry. Tang dynasty China's greatest lyric voice, Li Bai wrote roughly 1,000 surviving poems celebrating wine, friendship, and nature. He killed several men as a young knight-errant, drank with emperors, and legend says he drowned reaching for the moon's reflection.

story.name: Li Bai
story.description: Born on the Silk Road in Kyrgyzstan, summoned to compose poetry for the Tang emperor, exiled for offending the imperial consort, then caught in the An Lushan Rebellion. China's wine-drinking, sword-fighting poet laureate.

moments.name: Li Bai Is Born on the Silk Road in Central Asia
moments.subtitle: The future poet's merchant family lives at the frontier of Tang dynasty China
moments.description: Around 701 CE, the poet Li Bai was born in Suyab, an ancient Silk Road city in present-day Kyrgyzstan, where his family had prospered in trade at the frontier of Tang dynasty China. When Li Bai was about five, his father secretly moved the family to Sichuan near Chengdu, under circumstances that remain mysterious due to a lack of legal authorization for the move. The young Li Bai grew up reading Confucian classics, composing poetry before age ten, and practicing swordsmanship. He killed several men in his youth as a knight-errant before turning fully to literature.

moments.name: Emperor Xuanzong Summons Li Bai to the Imperial Court in Chang'an
moments.subtitle: The emperor personally seasons the poet's soup at a banquet in his honor
moments.description: In 742 CE, Emperor Xuanzong summoned Li Bai to the imperial court in Chang'an (modern Xi'an) after hearing lavish praise from the Daoist priest Wu Yun. The poet He Zhizhang nicknamed Li Bai the Immortal Exiled from Heaven upon meeting him. The emperor was so impressed by Li Bai's abilities that he hosted a grand banquet and personally seasoned the poet's soup. Xuanzong appointed Li Bai to the Hanlin Academy, where he composed poetry for the court. Li Bai often arrived drunk but performed brilliantly on the spot, writing celebrated poems about the imperial consort Yang Guifei.

moments.name: Li Bai Is Dismissed from the Imperial Court After Offending a Powerful Eunuch
moments.subtitle: A drunken poet makes the most powerful eunuch in China remove his muddy boots
moments.description: Around 744 CE, Li Bai was politely dismissed from the Tang imperial court in Chang'an after making powerful enemies. According to a famous anecdote, the drunken poet once had the powerful eunuch Gao Lishi remove his muddy boots in front of the emperor. Gao Lishi took offense and later persuaded the imperial consort Yang Guifei that Li Bai's poems about her were insulting. At their urging, Emperor Xuanzong reluctantly sent Li Bai away with generous gifts of gold and silver. Li Bai formally became a Daoist and spent the following years wandering across China, composing some of his most celebrated verses.

moments.name: Li Bai Meets the Young Poet Du Fu in Luoyang
moments.subtitle: Chinese literature's two greatest poets form a friendship for the ages
moments.description: In 744 CE, shortly after his dismissal from court, Li Bai met the younger poet Du Fu in Luoyang, beginning one of the most celebrated friendships in Chinese literary history. Du Fu was 31 and relatively unknown; Li Bai was 43 and already famous across the empire. The two poets traveled together through Henan and Shandong, drinking, writing, and discussing poetry. Du Fu wrote numerous poems expressing admiration and affection for Li Bai, while Li Bai's references to Du Fu were fewer but warm. Their contrasting styles, Li Bai's romanticism against Du Fu's realism, would come to define Chinese poetry.

moments.name: Li Bai Dies at 61, Legendarily While Reaching for the Moon's Reflection
moments.subtitle: The Wine Immortal's death spawns a myth as famous as any of his 1,000 surviving poems
moments.description: In 762 CE, Li Bai died at the age of 61 in Dangtu, Anhui province, while staying with a relative. The historical cause of death is uncertain, but the most famous legend holds that the drunken poet drowned after leaning from a boat to embrace the moon's reflection in the Yangtze River. Around 1,000 of Li Bai's poems survive, including works still memorized by Chinese schoolchildren today. His friend Du Fu outlived him by eight years but never recovered from the loss. Li Bai's nickname, the Immortal of Poetry, proved prophetic: his verses remain central to Chinese literature 1,200 years later.
